extraction.name: CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition
extraction.description: The CoNLL-2003 named entity data consists of eight files covering two languages, English and German. For each language there is a training file, a development file, a test file and a large file with unannotated data. The task concentrates on four types of named entities: persons, locations, organizations and miscellaneous entities.
extraction.creator: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder
extraction.citeAs: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder. 2003. Introduction to the CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset consists of English and German named entity data prepared for the CoNLL-2003 shared task. The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus, consisting of Reuters news stories. The German data was taken from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus, extracted from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau. For each language there is a training file, a development file, a test file and a large file with unannotated data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: English raw data came from the Reuters Corpus, consisting of Reuters news stories. German raw data came from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus, from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau. The unannotated data contain 17 million tokens for English and 14 million tokens for German.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: English articles are from August 1996 to August 1997; training and development data were taken from ten days at the end of August 1996, test data from December 1996, and preprocessed raw data from September 1996. German training, development and test sets were taken from articles written in one week at the end of August 1992, and raw data were taken from September to December 1992.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The data was split into training, development, test, and unannotated files for each language. The split between development data and test data was chosen to avoid systems being tuned to the test data.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Before release to participants, linguistic preprocessing was applied: for all data, a tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and a chunker were applied to the raw data. Two basic language-specific tokenizers were created. The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger. The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by TreeTagger.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Named entity tagging of English and German training, development, and test data was done by hand at the University of Antwerp. Mostly, MUC conventions were followed. An extra named entity category called MISC was added to denote names not in the other categories, including adjectives like Italian and events like 1000 Lakes Rally. The data uses the IOB tagging scheme with entity types PER, ORG, LOC and MISC. Named entities are assumed to be non-recursive and non-overlapping; when an entity is embedded in another, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Mostly, MUC conventions were followed. The tagging scheme is IOB: words outside entities are tagged O, words inside an entity are tagged I-XXX, and when two entities of the same type are adjacent, the first word of the second entity is tagged B-XXX. When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: MBT tagger for English; TreeTagger for German.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The MISC category is very diverse. Named entities are assumed to be non-recursive and non-overlapping. When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The training data were used to train learning methods, the development data could be used for tuning parameters, the test data were used for evaluation, and the large unannotated files were intended to be incorporated into the learning process in one way or another.
